question: When image-reconstruction training data and model capacity are scaled together, do denoising, accelerated MRI, and super-resolution retain power-law gains large enough to justify millions of examples?

key_findings.claim: In-distribution denoising gains flatten after only thousands of clean training images for both convolutional and transformer restorers.
key_findings.evidence: For U-Net, the fitted PSNR exponent falls from 0.0048 up to about 6,000 images to 0.0019 beyond that; for SwinIR it falls from 0.0050 to 0.0017. Model-size sweeps are used to reduce capacity bottleneck confounding.

anchors.section: Robustness of our finding of slowing scaling laws

key_findings.claim: Scaling SwinIR still yields measurable state-of-the-art gains, but architecture choice is much more consequential than the extrapolated data-only gain.
key_findings.evidence: The largest 129M-parameter SwinIR trained on 100,000 images improves four denoising sets by 0.05--0.22 dB. Extrapolating the flatter U-Net fit would require about 150M images merely to reach the observed SwinIR level, under the optimistic assumption that the slope does not flatten further.

anchors.section: B Benchmarking our models for Gaussian image denoising, Table 3

key_findings.claim: Accelerated MRI and super-resolution exhibit the same two-regime pattern at different data scales.
key_findings.evidence: For 4x fastMRI brain reconstruction, the best U-Net SSIM exponent drops from 0.0072 through roughly 2,500 images to 0.0026 from 5,000 onward. For 2x super-resolution, the PSNR exponent drops from 0.0075 through about 30,000 images to 0.0029 from 60,000 onward.

anchors.section: 4 Empirical scaling laws for compressive sensing
C Empirical scaling laws for image super-resolution with a U-Net

key_findings.claim: A low-dimensional linear model explains flattening as finite-sample signal-model error becoming smaller than an irreducible noise floor.
key_findings.evidence: The PCA estimator's risk is bounded by optimal risk plus a term proportional to (d+n sigma squared) log(n)/N. The early-stopped gradient-descent bound similarly separates a noise-dependent floor from terms decreasing with sample size.

key_findings.claim: The conclusion is deliberately narrower than a general claim that more reconstruction data no longer helps.
key_findings.evidence: The study covers three supervised tasks, two architecture families, PSNR/SSIM, and in-distribution tests. The authors explicitly leave perceptual quality, self-supervised scaling, and robustness from larger, more diverse datasets unresolved.

method.core_idea: Empirically fit piecewise data-scaling curves only after optimizing network size at every dataset size, then interpret the slowdown with a solvable subspace-denoising model.
method.mechanism: Construct nested datasets, train multiple U-Net or SwinIR capacities per size, select the best validation configuration, fit log-log performance exponents before and after the observed bend, and compare finite-sample bounds with a noise floor.
assumptions: The best tested width at each dataset size is close enough to the capacity optimum
Nested ImageNet or fastMRI subsets preserve the relevant in-distribution data law
Local fitted power laws remain informative for cautious extrapolation
PSNR and SSIM capture the reconstruction improvements of interest
A linear low-dimensional denoising model captures the qualitative origin of neural-network saturation

techniques.role: Prevents a fixed undersized network from masquerading as a data-scaling plateau.
Quantifies the transition from an initial power-law regime to a much flatter regime.
Separates finite-sample estimation error from irreducible measurement noise in a tractable model.
Reduces distribution changes when comparing different dataset sizes.

evaluations.setting: Gaussian color denoising on ImageNet subsets from 100 to 100,000 images
evaluations.metric: PSNR after optimizing U-Net or SwinIR size
evaluations.result: exponents flatten from 0.0048 to 0.0019 for U-Net and from 0.0050 to 0.0017 for SwinIR; the largest SwinIR adds 0.05--0.22 dB on four standard sets
evaluations.baseline: smaller datasets and capacities, U-Net, original SwinIR, and SCUNet

evaluations.setting: single-contrast fastMRI brain, 4x multi-coil acceleration, 50 to 50,000 images
evaluations.metric: SSIM of the best U-Net capacity
evaluations.result: the fitted exponent falls from 0.0072 below roughly 2,500 images to 0.0026 above 5,000
evaluations.baseline: smaller nested training subsets and alternative U-Net widths

evaluations.metric: PSNR of the best U-Net capacity
evaluations.result: the fitted exponent falls from 0.0075 up to about 30,000 images to 0.0029 from 60,000 images onward
evaluations.baseline: smaller nested training subsets and alternative U-Net widths

evaluations.setting: simulated d-dimensional Gaussian subspace denoising in ambient dimension n
evaluations.result: PCA and early-stopped empirical-risk estimators approach a noise-dependent floor as N grows

limitations: Author-stated: results cover three reconstruction problems and two architecture families, not all inverse problems or model designs.
Author-stated: PSNR and SSIM may miss perceptual improvements that more data could produce.
Author-stated: evaluation is in-distribution; diverse large datasets may still materially improve out-of-distribution robustness.
Author-stated: supervised scaling need not predict self-supervised scaling.
Extrapolations over many orders of magnitude assume a fitted local slope persists even though the paper's central observation is that slopes change.
The linear subspace theory provides a qualitative mechanism, not a bound for the nonlinear U-Net and SwinIR experiments.
failure_modes: The apparent plateau is caused by an untested architecture or optimization bottleneck rather than a task error floor.
A larger dataset changes coverage, patient diversity, scanner physics, or corruptions instead of drawing more samples from the same distribution.
A perceptually meaningful improvement is invisible to PSNR or SSIM.
Selection over many capacities and learning schedules overfits the validation set at some dataset sizes.
Power-law extrapolation crosses into a new regime before reaching the projected scale.
reusable_insights: Scale data and capacity jointly before attributing a plateau to data saturation.
Report bends in a scaling curve rather than forcing a single exponent across all scales.
Express data value relative to the irreducible error floor and the metric actually optimized.
Distinguish more same-distribution samples from broader data coverage; they answer different robustness questions.
Compare the projected gain from data scaling with achievable architecture improvements and acquisition cost.
open_questions: Do perceptual, clinical, and distribution-shift metrics continue improving after PSNR or SSIM flattens?
How do self-supervised and foundation-model reconstruction methods scale with unlabeled measurements?
Can a small-scale experiment reliably detect future regime changes rather than merely extrapolate the current slope?
Which task properties determine the bend point and post-bend exponent?
Does patient- and volume-level effective sample size explain medical reconstruction scaling better than slice count?

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically
competitive_landscape.difference: Hestness et al. characterize power laws across language, classification, image processing, and speech and observe architecture-independent slopes; this paper isolates supervised inverse imaging and emphasizes an early transition toward a task error floor while jointly tuning capacity.

competitive_landscape.title: A Constructive Prediction of the Generalization Error Across Scales
competitive_landscape.difference: Rosenfeld et al. fit a saturating functional form across vision and language while varying model and dataset scale; this work measures task-specific reconstruction bends and supplies a denoising error-floor argument.

competitive_landscape.title: SwinIR: Image Restoration Using Swin Transformer
competitive_landscape.difference: SwinIR establishes a transformer restoration model and strong task benchmarks; this paper varies SwinIR capacity and data together to measure whether its denoising advantage continues scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: End-to-End Variational Networks for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
competitive_landscape.difference: The variational network builds measurement physics into an unrolled fastMRI reconstructor and targets absolute performance; the scaling paper uses a direct U-Net reconstruction pipeline to isolate dataset- and width-dependent SSIM trends.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: This is a principled joint model-and-data scaling study across denoising, accelerated MRI, and super-resolution, supported by a theoretical denoising model that explains early flattening.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Large nested data and capacity grids reveal consistent two-regime curves, and two linear-estimator bounds separate finite-data error from a noise floor.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The cross-task evidence that standard in-distribution reconstruction metrics flatten at moderate data scale is useful and more directly decision-relevant than generic scaling laws. It does not justify a universal ceiling on data value: the strongest unresolved alternatives are distribution coverage, perceptual or clinical metrics, self-supervision, and better physics-aware architectures.

reviewer_notes: Read all 47 extracted pages, including experimental appendices and proofs, with a second pass on fitted regimes, capacity controls, theorem assumptions, benchmark tables, and stated limitations. Primary records for Hestness scaling, Rosenfeld scaling, SwinIR, and end-to-end MRI variational networks were checked.
